# Italian Alphabet & Phonetics

Italian uses the 21-letter Latin alphabet (j, k, w, x, y appear only in loanwords). Each letter maps to a small, predictable set of sounds — read what you see, with stable vowels and a few consonant rules to learn. Italian is famously *transparent*: once you know the rules, you can pronounce any word.

## Core Vocabulary

| Lettera | Pronunciation | Note |
|---------|--------------|------|
| a | "ah" | always *ah* — *casa* (KAH-zah) |
| e | "eh" or "ay" | open vs closed; varies by region |
| i | "ee" | *vino* (VEE-noh) |
| o | "oh" | open vs closed; *sole* / *come* |
| u | "oo" | *luna* (LOO-nah) |
| c + a/o/u | "k" | *casa, cosa, cuore* |
| c + e/i | "ch" | *cena* (CHEH-nah), *cibo* (CHEE-boh) |
| ch + e/i | "k" | *che* (KEH), *chi* (KEE) |
| g + a/o/u | "g" (hard) | *gatto, gola, gusto* |
| g + e/i | "j" | *gelato* (jeh-LAH-toh) |
| gh + e/i | "g" (hard) | *spaghetti* (spah-GHET-tee) |
| gn | "ny" | *gnocchi* (NYOK-kee) |
| gl + i | "lyi" | *figlio* (FEEL-yoh) |
| sc + a/o/u | "sk" | *scuola* (SKWOH-lah) |
| sc + e/i | "sh" | *scemo* (SHEH-moh) |
| z | "ts" or "dz" | *pizza* (PEET-tsah), *zero* (DZEH-roh) |
| h | silent | exists only in spelling (*ho, hai*) |
| double consonants | held longer | *anno* (an-NO) ≠ *ano* (AH-no) |
| r | trilled | tip-of-tongue tap, like Spanish |

## Example Sentences

- **Buongiorno!** (bwon-JOR-noh) — Good morning!
- **Mi chiamo Marco.** (mee KYAH-moh MAR-koh) — My name is Marco.
- **Una pizza margherita, per favore.** (mar-gheh-REE-tah) — A margherita pizza, please.
- **Quanti anni hai?** (KWAN-tee AN-nee EYE) — How old are you?
- **Cinque, sei, sette.** (CHEEN-kweh, SEH-ee, SET-teh) — Five, six, seven.
- **Gli gnocchi sono deliziosi.** (lyi NYOK-kee SOH-noh deh-lee-tsee-OH-zee) — The gnocchi are delicious.
- **Andiamo a Roma.** (an-DYAH-moh ah ROH-mah) — Let's go to Rome.

## Grammar / Pronunciation Notes

**The c/g rule.** Before *a, o, u* the letters *c* and *g* are hard (k, g). Before *e, i* they soften (ch, j). To force a hard sound before *e/i*, Italians insert *h*: *che* (KEH), *spaghetti* (spah-GHET-tee). To force a soft sound before *a/o/u*, they insert *i*: *ciao* (CHOW), *giorno* (JOR-noh) — the *i* is silent, just a marker.

**Double consonants are real.** Italians genuinely hold a doubled consonant longer than a single one, and the meaning often changes: *casa* (house) vs *cassa* (cash register), *pena* (punishment) vs *penna* (pen), *nono* (ninth) vs *nonno* (grandfather).

**Vowels are pure.** Unlike English, Italian vowels don't drift into diphthongs. *o* in *sole* is one steady sound, not the *oh-oo* glide English speakers add. Practice keeping each vowel short and crisp.

**The silent h.** *H* is never pronounced in Italian. It exists in *ho, hai, ha, hanno* (forms of *avere*) only to distinguish them in writing from *o* (or), *ai* (to the), *a* (to), *anno* (year).

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't anglicize** *r*: it's a tip-of-tongue tap, never the English retroflex.
- **Don't shorten** doubled consonants: *anno* (year) and *ano* (anus) are different words.
- **Don't pronounce** *ch* like English "ch": Italian *ch* = English "k". *Chi* sounds like "kee", not "chee".
- **Don't drop** vowels at the end of words. Italian words almost always end in a vowel that must be voiced — *libro* is "LEE-broh", not "LEE-br".
- **Don't pronounce** the *i* in *ciao*, *giorno*, *gli* as a separate vowel — it's just a soft-c/g marker.

## Try It Yourself

1. Read aloud: *casa, cassa, pena, penna, nono, nonno*. Hear the doubled consonants.
2. Pronounce: *gnocchi, gli, figlio, sogno, lasagne*. Master *gn* and *gl*.
3. Practice the c/g rule: *casa / cena / che — gatto / gelato / ghetto*.
4. Spell your name with the Italian phonetic alphabet (Ancona, Bologna, Como...).
5. Read this sentence aloud three times: *La giraffa giapponese mangia gnocchi al cioccolato.*

## Next Steps

Move to *Greetings & Introductions* to put your pronunciation to work in real conversation, and to *Stress, Accents & Intonation* to learn how Italian stresses words and uses written accents.

# Greetings & Introductions

Italians greet warmly and follow clear rules of register: *ciao* between friends, *buongiorno* / *buonasera* with strangers and elders, plus a kiss on each cheek among acquaintances. Getting these rituals right is half of sounding fluent — words alone aren't enough without the right setting.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Register |
|----------|---------|----------|
| ciao | hi / bye | informal, friends |
| salve | hi (neutral) | polite, anyone |
| buongiorno | good morning / good day | until ~3pm, formal |
| buon pomeriggio | good afternoon | after lunch |
| buonasera | good evening | after ~5pm |
| buonanotte | good night | only when leaving / going to bed |
| arrivederci | goodbye (formal) | with strangers, shops |
| arrivederLa | goodbye (very formal) | to one elder/professional |
| a presto / a dopo | see you soon / later | informal |
| a domani | see you tomorrow | |
| come stai? | how are you? (informal *tu*) | |
| come sta? | how are you? (formal *Lei*) | |
| come va? | how's it going? | very informal |
| bene, grazie | well, thanks | |
| così così | so-so | |
| non c'è male | not bad | |
| piacere (di conoscerti) | nice to meet you | |
| mi chiamo... | my name is... | |
| sono di... | I'm from... | |
| ho ... anni | I am ... years old | |
| ti presento... | let me introduce you to... | informal |
| Le presento... | let me introduce you to... | formal |
| scusa / scusi | sorry / excuse me | informal / formal |
| prego | you're welcome / please / go ahead | multi-purpose |
| per favore / per piacere | please | |
| grazie (mille) | thank you (very much) | |

## Example Sentences

- **Ciao, come stai? — Bene, grazie. E tu?** — Hi, how are you? — Well, thanks. And you?
- **Buongiorno, signora. Come sta?** — Good morning, ma'am. How are you? (formal)
- **Mi chiamo Anna, sono di Firenze.** — My name is Anna, I'm from Florence.
- **Piacere di conoscerla. Sono Marco Rossi.** — Pleased to meet you. I'm Marco Rossi. (formal)
- **Ti presento il mio amico Luca.** — Let me introduce you to my friend Luca.
- **Ho ventidue anni. E tu?** — I'm 22 years old. And you?
- **Scusi, parla inglese?** — Excuse me, do you speak English? (formal)
- **Arrivederci, a presto!** — Goodbye, see you soon!

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Tu vs Lei.** This is the central social distinction in Italian. *Tu* is for friends, family, children, peers; *Lei* (capitalized in formal writing) is for strangers, elders, professionals, anyone you'd address as "Mr./Ms." in English. *Lei* uses the third-person singular conjugation of the verb: *come sta?* (literally "how does she stand?"). Defaulting to *Lei* with adults you don't know is always safe.

**Time-of-day greetings.** *Buongiorno* covers morning through early afternoon (until ~3pm). *Buon pomeriggio* is afternoon (rare in conversation). *Buonasera* starts roughly when the sun sets — anywhere from 4pm in winter to 8pm in summer. *Buonanotte* is reserved for *leaving* late at night or going to bed; never use it as a greeting.

**Prego is everywhere.** It means "you're welcome" (response to *grazie*), "please" (when offering: *prego, si accomodi* = please, take a seat), "after you" (waving someone through a door), or "what can I do for you?" (a shopkeeper opening). Context tells you which.

**Body language matters.** *Ciao* is often paired with two cheek kisses (*due baci*) — left cheek first, then right — among friends and family. With strangers, a handshake. Italians stand closer in conversation than English speakers; don't back away.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't say** *ciao* to your boss, your professor, or a shopkeeper you've just met. Use *salve* or *buongiorno*.
- **Don't use** *buonanotte* as "good night, hope you have a nice evening" — it specifically means "I'm going to sleep now."
- **Avoid** *Sono dieci anni* — Italian uses *avere* (to have) for age: *Ho dieci anni* (literally "I have ten years").
- **Don't translate** "What's your name?" word-for-word. Italians say *Come ti chiami?* (informal, "what do you call yourself?") or *Come si chiama?* (formal).
- **Don't conflate** *ti presento* (informal *tu*) and *Le presento* (formal *Lei*) — match the register to the person you're addressing.

## Try It Yourself

1. Greet five different people: a child, your friend, your professor, a shopkeeper, your grandmother. Use the right register for each.
2. Introduce yourself in 4 sentences: name, age, hometown, one fun fact (*sono di...*, *ho ... anni*, *mi piace...*).
3. Practice the two registers side by side: *Ciao, come stai?* / *Buongiorno, come sta?*
4. Memorize the greeting-by-time-of-day rule and apply it for one full day.
5. Role-play meeting someone: greet, introduce yourself, ask their name and where they're from, exchange a *piacere*.

## Next Steps

Move to *Stress, Accents & Intonation* to handle the rhythm of Italian sentences, and to *Gender, Articles & Noun Plurals* to start building real Italian phrases beyond fixed greetings.

# Stress, Accents & Intonation

Italian stress is mostly on the second-to-last syllable, but exceptions are common — and getting stress wrong can change meaning or make you incomprehensible. Written accents (*à è é ì ò ù*) mark the few cases where stress lands on the last syllable, and they're never optional.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | Stress pattern | Note |
|----------|----------------|------|
| **parole piane** | penultimate (default) | *amico, casa, finestra* |
| **parole tronche** | final, written accent | *città, caffè, perché* |
| **parole sdrucciole** | antepenultimate | *medico, telefono, sabato* |
| **parole bisdrucciole** | fourth-from-end | *telefonano, dimenticano* |
| à | "ah" with stress on this syllable | *città* (chee-TAH) |
| è | "eh" open + stress | *caffè* (kahf-FEH) |
| é | "ay" closed + stress | *perché* (per-KAY) |
| ì | "ee" + stress | *così* (koh-ZEE) |
| ò | "oh" open + stress | *però* (peh-ROH) |
| ù | "oo" + stress | *più* (PYOO) |
| è (verb form) | is | *Lui è italiano* |
| e | and | *pane e acqua* |
| sì | yes | accented to distinguish from *si* (oneself) |
| dà | gives (verb) | distinguishes from *da* (from/by) |
| là / lì | there | distinguishes from *la / li* (articles) |
| qui / qua | here | NO accent — never accented in standard spelling |

## Example Sentences

- **La città è bellissima.** (CHEET-tah / EH / bel-LEES-see-mah) — The city is beautiful.
- **Perché studi italiano? — Perché lo amo!** (per-KAY / per-KAY) — Why do you study Italian? — Because I love it!
- **Vorrei un caffè, per favore.** (kahf-FEH) — I'd like a coffee, please.
- **Sì, sono italiano. Di Milano.** (SEE / SOH-noh) — Yes, I'm Italian. From Milan.
- **Il medico arriva sabato.** (MEH-dee-koh / SAH-bah-toh) — The doctor arrives Saturday.
- **Telefono al telefono di mia madre.** (teh-LEH-foh-noh / teh-LEH-foh-noh) — I phone on my mother's phone.
- **Dove abiti? — Lì, in via Roma.** (LEE) — Where do you live? — There, on Roma Street.

## Grammar / Stress Rules

**The default is penultimate.** ~80% of Italian words stress the second-to-last syllable: *a-MI-co, fi-NES-tra, in-SIE-me*. Treat this as the rule and learn the exceptions.

**Words ending in a stressed vowel always carry a written accent.** *città, caffè, virtù, perché*. Without the accent the stress shifts and the word changes meaning or becomes nonsense.

**è vs é.** Both mark a stressed *e* on the final syllable, but they distinguish two sounds: *è* is "open" (mouth wider, like English "bed") and *é* is "closed" (mouth tighter, like English "bay"). The two most common: *è* = "is" (verb), *perché* = "why/because". Mixing them up is a literacy giveaway.

**Antepenultimate stress (*sdrucciole*) is unmarked but common.** Many words stress the third-from-last syllable: *MEdico, TElefono, SAbato, MUsica, AUtomobile*. There's no written marker — you have to learn each one.

**Verb stress shifts the meaning.** *àncora* (anchor, noun, antepenultimate) vs *ancóra* (still, again, adverb, penultimate). *parli* (you speak, present) vs *parlò* (he/she spoke, past, accented). Context usually disambiguates, but stress is part of the meaning.

**Intonation: rising for questions.** Italian yes/no questions have the same word order as statements; only intonation changes. *Parli italiano.* (statement, falling) vs *Parli italiano?* (question, rising at the end). Wh-questions (with *come, dove, perché, chi*) keep a falling intonation.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't omit** the written accent on *è, perché, città, caffè* — it's a real spelling error.
- **Don't write** *qui* with an accent — it has none. Same for *qua, su, no*.
- **Don't confuse** *é* and *è* in writing: *perché* (closed *é*), *è* the verb (open *è*). Most native speakers also use *è* as a fallback when uncertain — bad habit, but common.
- **Don't move stress** from antepenultimate to penultimate on *sdrucciole* words: it's *MEdico*, never *meDIco*.
- **Don't treat** Italian intonation as flat — questions need a clear rise; statements need a clear fall. Without these, you sound robotic.

## Try It Yourself

1. Mark the stress on these words: *finestra, telefono, città, perché, sabato, automobile, parlerò, ancora*.
2. Read aloud: *Perché la città è così bella?* Pay attention to every accent.
3. Practice questions vs statements with the same words: *Parli italiano* vs *Parli italiano?*
4. Find five *parole sdrucciole* in a paragraph of Italian text and read them aloud with the right stress.
5. Listen to an Italian news clip and trace the intonation curve — where do voices rise, where do they fall?

## Next Steps

Move to *Gender, Articles & Noun Plurals* to start building Italian noun phrases now that you can pronounce them, and to *Adjectives & Agreement* to practice the agreement chains.

# Gender, Articles & Noun Plurals

Every Italian noun has a gender — masculine or feminine — and the article, adjective, and sometimes verb agree with it. Getting gender right is the single biggest leap from English; once it clicks, every other agreement chain follows naturally.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | Gender | Plural | Note |
|----------|--------|--------|------|
| il libro | m. | i libri | -o → -i |
| la casa | f. | le case | -a → -e |
| il fiore | m. | i fiori | -e → -i |
| la chiave | f. | le chiavi | -e nouns can be either gender |
| lo studente | m. (s+cons.) | gli studenti | *lo* before s+consonant, z, ps, gn |
| l'amico | m. | gli amici | *l'* before vowel (m. plural *gli*) |
| l'amica | f. | le amiche | *l'* before vowel; plural needs *h* to keep hard *c* |
| un libro | m. indef. | dei libri | "a/some" |
| una casa | f. indef. | delle case | "a/some" |
| uno studente | m. indef. | degli studenti | *uno* before s+cons., z |
| un'amica | f. indef. before vowel | delle amiche | apostrophe only on feminine before vowel |
| la mano | f. (irregular) | le mani | exception — looks masculine but is feminine |
| il problema | m. (irregular) | i problemi | Greek-origin -ma nouns are masculine |
| il sistema | m. (irregular) | i sistemi | same: -ma + masc. |
| il cinema | m. (invariable) | i cinema | foreign-origin, doesn't change |
| la città | f. (invariable) | le città | accented final vowel → invariable |
| il caffè | m. (invariable) | i caffè | same rule |
| il film | m. (invariable) | i film | foreign loanword |
| lo zio | m. | gli zii | *z* takes *lo / gli* |

## Example Sentences

- **Il libro è interessante.** — The book is interesting.
- **Le case in Italia sono colorate.** — Houses in Italy are colorful.
- **Ho un amico italiano e un'amica spagnola.** — I have an Italian (m) friend and a Spanish (f) friend.
- **Gli studenti studiano con lo zio.** — The students study with the uncle.
- **La mano destra. Le mani forti.** — The right hand. Strong hands.
- **Il problema è chiaro. I problemi sono molti.** — The problem is clear. The problems are many.
- **Vorrei un caffè e una pizza.** — I'd like a coffee and a pizza.

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Default gender from ending.** Most nouns ending in *-o* are masculine (*il libro, il treno*); most ending in *-a* are feminine (*la casa, la donna*). Nouns ending in *-e* split — you have to learn each one (*il fiore* m., *la chiave* f.). Plurals: *-o → -i, -a → -e, -e → -i*.

**Choosing the article.** Italian has more article forms than English. The right one depends on gender, number, and the first sound of the next word:
- masculine singular: *il* (most words), *lo* (before s+cons., z, ps, gn, x), *l'* (before vowel)
- masculine plural: *i* (most), *gli* (before s+cons., z, vowel)
- feminine singular: *la* (most), *l'* (before vowel)
- feminine plural: *le* (always)

**Indefinite articles** follow the same pattern: *un* (most masc.), *uno* (s+cons., z), *un'* (fem. before vowel), *una* (most fem.).

**Plural spelling tricks.**
- Words ending in *-co/-go* (hard c/g): keep the hard sound by inserting *h* — *amico → amici* (BUT *medico → medici*, irregular). Two-syllable words tend to stay hard (*chic-o → chichi*); longer words tend to soften (*medico → medici*). Memorize the common ones.
- Words ending in *-ca/-ga* (feminine, hard c/g): always insert *h* — *amica → amiche, banca → banche*.
- Words ending in *-cia/-gia*: drop the *i* if a consonant precedes (*spiaggia → spiagge*); keep it if a vowel does (*ciliegia → ciliegie*).

**Invariable nouns** don't change in the plural: words ending in accented vowel (*città, caffè, virtù*), foreign loans (*film, sport, computer*), single-letter abbreviations (*il km, i km*). The article is the only signal of plural.

**Tricky genders.**
- *la mano, la radio, la moto, la foto* — feminine despite ending in *-o* (often shortened from longer feminine words: *la moto* = *la motocicletta*).
- *il problema, il sistema, il programma, il poema, il tema* — masculine despite ending in *-a* (Greek origin).
- *il poeta, il pilota, il turista* — masculine -*a* nouns referring to people.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't say** *il studente* — before *s+consonant*, use *lo studente*.
- **Don't use** *la* before vowel sounds: it's *l'amica*, not *la amica*.
- **Don't apostrophize** *un* before masculine nouns: *un amico* (no apostrophe), but *un'amica* (apostrophe).
- **Don't drop** the *h* in feminine plurals of *-ca/-ga* words: *banche*, not *bance*.
- **Don't forget** the article. Italian uses articles where English drops them: *Mi piace **la** pizza*, *Studio **l'**italiano*.

## Try It Yourself

1. Find the gender of these nouns from context: *il problema, la mano, lo studente, l'università, il film*.
2. Make plurals: *amico, amica, banca, medico, città, caffè, ragazzo, ragazza*.
3. Pick the right article: *___ zaino, ___ zia, ___ amici, ___ amiche, ___ studenti*.
4. Translate: "the books, a problem, the cities, an Italian (f) friend, the doctors".
5. Memorize 10 nouns with their gender and article. Use them in a sentence each.

## Next Steps

Move to *Adjectives & Agreement* to make adjectives agree with the gendered nouns you now know, and to *Present Tense: Regular & Irregular* to put nouns and verbs together in real sentences.

# Present Tense: Regular & Irregular

The present tense (*presente indicativo*) covers what English needs three forms for: "I eat", "I am eating", "I do eat" — all just *mangio*. Italian has three regular conjugation classes (*-are, -ere, -ire*) and several high-frequency irregular verbs you'll meet on day one.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Pattern |
|----------|---------|---------|
| **-ARE: parlare** | to speak | parl**o**, parl**i**, parl**a**, parl**iamo**, parl**ate**, parl**ano** |
| **-ERE: vedere** | to see | ved**o**, ved**i**, ved**e**, ved**iamo**, ved**ete**, ved**ono** |
| **-IRE: dormire** | to sleep | dorm**o**, dorm**i**, dorm**e**, dorm**iamo**, dorm**ite**, dorm**ono** |
| **-IRE (-isc-): finire** | to finish | fin**isco**, fin**isci**, fin**isce**, fin**iamo**, fin**ite**, fin**iscono** |
| essere | to be | sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono |
| avere | to have | ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno |
| andare | to go | vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno |
| venire | to come | vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono |
| fare | to do/make | faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno |
| dire | to say | dico, dici, dice, diciamo, dite, dicono |
| dare | to give | do, dai, dà, diamo, date, danno |
| stare | to stay/be | sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno |
| sapere | to know (a fact) | so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno |
| volere | to want | voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono |
| potere | to be able to | posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono |
| dovere | to have to / must | devo, devi, deve, dobbiamo, dovete, devono |
| uscire | to go out | esco, esci, esce, usciamo, uscite, escono |
| bere | to drink | bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono |

## Example Sentences

- **Parlo italiano da due anni.** — I've been speaking Italian for two years.
- **Cosa fai stasera? — Vado al cinema.** — What are you doing tonight? — I'm going to the cinema.
- **Mio fratello ha vent'anni.** — My brother is twenty.
- **Capiamo perfettamente.** — We understand perfectly.
- **Vogliono un caffè.** — They want a coffee.
- **Non posso venire domani, devo lavorare.** — I can't come tomorrow, I have to work.
- **Beviamo il vino con la cena.** — We drink wine with dinner.
- **Sai dov'è il museo?** — Do you know where the museum is?

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**The three regular conjugations** end in *-are, -ere, -ire*. Drop the ending and add the right personal endings:
- *-are*: -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano
- *-ere*: -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono
- *-ire*: -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ite, -ono

The *-iamo* ("we") ending is the same across all three classes.

**The -isc- subgroup of -ire.** Many *-ire* verbs insert *-isc-* in singular and 3rd-plural forms: *finire → finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono*. Other *-isc-* verbs: *capire* (understand), *preferire* (prefer), *spedire* (send), *pulire* (clean). The *-iamo* and *-ite* "we/you-pl" forms keep no *-isc-*. Pure *-ire* verbs (no *-isc-*): *dormire, partire, sentire, aprire, offrire*.

**Subject pronouns are usually dropped.** Italian endings make the subject clear, so *io, tu, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro* are used only for emphasis or contrast: *Io parlo italiano, ma lui parla francese* (I speak Italian, but he speaks French).

**Present tense covers continuous and habitual.** *Mangio adesso* (I'm eating right now), *Mangio sempre alle otto* (I always eat at eight). Italian also has a true progressive: *Sto mangiando* (I am [in the act of] eating) — used when emphasising the moment.

**Modal verbs (*potere, dovere, volere, sapere*)** behave like English modals — followed by an infinitive: *Posso entrare?* (May I come in?), *Devo studiare* (I have to study), *Voglio dormire* (I want to sleep), *So nuotare* (I know how to swim).

**Avere vs essere for "I am".** *Sono americano* (I am American) — identity. *Ho venti anni* (I am twenty) — age uses *avere* in Italian. *Ho fame, ho sete, ho freddo, ho caldo, ho paura, ho ragione, ho torto* — physical/emotional states all use *avere*.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't translate** "I am twenty years old" with *sono* — it's *Ho vent'anni*.
- **Don't say** *Io vado* every time you mean "I go" — drop *io* unless you're contrasting.
- **Don't insert** *-isc-* in *we/you-pl*: it's *finiamo, finite*, NOT *finisciamo, finiscite*.
- **Don't conjugate** *fare/dire/dare* like *-are* verbs: they're irregular. *Fanno*, not *farono*.
- **Don't translate** "I am eating" only with *Sto mangiando* — *Mangio* is correct in most contexts.

## Try It Yourself

1. Conjugate *parlare, vedere, dormire, finire* fully.
2. Pick five irregular verbs and conjugate them for *io, tu, lei, noi, voi, loro*.
3. Translate using *avere*: "I'm hungry", "She's twenty", "We're cold", "They're afraid".
4. Make 5 sentences with modals + infinitive: *Devo + V*, *Posso + V*, *Voglio + V*.
5. Tell what you typically do on a Sunday in 5 sentences using the present tense.

## Next Steps

Move to *Adjectives & Agreement* to add descriptive detail to your sentences, and to *Past Tenses: Passato Prossimo & Imperfetto* to talk about yesterday and your childhood.

# Adjectives & Agreement

Italian adjectives agree with the noun they describe in gender (m/f) and number (sg/pl). Most go *after* the noun, but a small set goes before with a specific meaning shift. Mastering agreement chains makes your Italian sound natural; getting them wrong is the most audible mistake learners make.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | Endings | Example |
|----------|---------|---------|
| **4-form (-o):** alto | alto/a/i/e | *un ragazzo alto, una ragazza alta, ragazzi alti, ragazze alte* |
| **2-form (-e):** grande | grande/i | *un libro grande, una casa grande, libri grandi, case grandi* |
| **invariable:** rosa | (no change) | *una rosa rosa, dei vestiti rosa* (foreign or color-of-thing) |
| bello | bello/a/i/e (irregular before noun) | adapts like *quello* before noun |
| buono | buono/a/i/e (sg. like *un/uno*) | *buon amico, buon giorno, buona sera* |
| nuovo | nuovo/a/i/e | new |
| vecchio | vecchio/a/i/e | old |
| giovane | giovane/i | young |
| simpatico | simpatico/a/ci/che | nice (4-form, plurals shift c→ch) |
| antipatico | antipatico/a/ci/che | unpleasant |
| stanco | stanco/a/chi/che | tired |
| difficile | difficile/i | difficult |
| facile | facile/i | easy |
| interessante | interessante/i | interesting |
| importante | importante/i | important |
| italiano | italiano/a/i/e | Italian (lowercase!) |
| **Position-shifting:** un grande uomo | a great man | *grande* before = "great" |
| un uomo grande | a big man | *grande* after = "big" |
| una vecchia amica | an old friend (long-time) | *vecchia* before = "long-standing" |
| una amica vecchia | an old (in age) friend | *vecchia* after = "elderly" |
| il mio caro amico | my dear friend | *caro* before = "beloved" |
| un appartamento caro | an expensive apartment | *caro* after = "expensive" |

## Example Sentences

- **La pizza italiana è buonissima.** — Italian pizza is delicious.
- **Ho due amici simpatici e tre amiche simpatiche.** — I have two nice (m) friends and three nice (f) friends.
- **Il mio nuovo lavoro è interessante.** — My new job is interesting.
- **Sono molto stanca oggi.** — I'm very tired today. (speaker is feminine)
- **Buongiorno! Buona giornata!** — Good morning! Have a good day!
- **Una donna vecchia entra nella vecchia casa.** — An elderly woman enters the old (long-standing) house.
- **Le strade sono lunghe e strette.** — The streets are long and narrow.

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Two adjective classes by ending pattern.**
- **4-form** adjectives (most common): masculine sg *-o*, feminine sg *-a*, masculine pl *-i*, feminine pl *-e*. *bello, alto, italiano, simpatico*.
- **2-form** adjectives: same form for both genders in singular (*-e*), same for both in plural (*-i*). *grande, importante, difficile, giovane, intelligente*.

**Position: usually after, sometimes before.** Most descriptive adjectives follow the noun: *una macchina rossa* (a red car), *un libro interessante* (an interesting book). A small set of common adjectives precedes the noun and often takes special forms — *bello, buono, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio, giovane, lungo, breve, alto, basso*. With these, position changes nuance: *un grande uomo* (a great man, abstract) vs *un uomo grande* (a big man, physical).

**bello and quello are special** before a noun — they take forms parallel to the definite articles:
- *bel libro, bello studente, bell'amico, bei libri, begli studenti, begli amici, bella casa, belle case*
After a noun, *bello* uses regular *-o/-a/-i/-e* endings: *Il libro è bello*. *Le case sono belle*.

**buono before a singular noun** patterns like *un/uno*: *un buon amico, un buono studente, una buon'idea, una buona pizza*. After the noun and in plural, normal endings: *un libro buono*, *due buoni amici*.

**Adjectives of nationality and language are lowercase.** *italiano, francese, inglese, tedesco, spagnolo* — all lowercase, unlike English. They agree like normal adjectives: *un ragazzo italiano, una ragazza italiana*.

**Color adjectives.** Most agree (*rosso, giallo, verde, nero, bianco, blu* — *blu* is invariable). When the color is the name of an object (e.g. *rosa* = pink/rose, *viola* = purple/violet, *arancione* often invariable), it tends to be invariable: *un vestito rosa, dei vestiti rosa*.

**Spelling traps in plurals.** Adjectives in *-co/-go* may keep or soften the hard sound: *bianco → bianchi, simpatico → simpatici, lungo → lunghi*. Generally hard c/g stays in shorter words and softens in *-ico*. Adjectives in *-ca/-ga* always keep the hard sound: *bianca → bianche, lunga → lunghe*.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't keep** the masculine ending when describing a feminine noun: *una casa **bella***, not *una casa bello*.
- **Don't capitalize** *italiano, americano, inglese* etc. — only proper nouns are capitalized.
- **Watch position-sensitive adjectives**: *un povero uomo* = "an unfortunate man"; *un uomo povero* = "a poor (no money) man".
- **Don't use** *bello* like English "beautiful" — Italian uses it for things that are simply nice or good. *È un bel film* = "It's a nice film", not necessarily "stunning".
- **Don't forget** that the speaker's own gender affects adjectives applied to themselves: a woman says *Sono stanca*; a man says *Sono stanco*.

## Try It Yourself

1. Make all 4 forms agree: *un ragazzo alto, una ragazza ___, ragazzi ___, ragazze ___*.
2. Apply *bello* before each: *un ___ libro, un ___ studente, una ___ amica, dei ___ giorni*.
3. Translate: "two nice friends (f), an Italian car, the new houses, a difficult exam".
4. Practice position-shift adjectives: write sentences for *grande, vecchio, povero, caro* in both positions.
5. Describe yourself in 4 adjectives, agreeing with your gender (e.g. *Sono italiana, alta, simpatica, e un po' stanca*).

## Next Steps

Move to *Numbers, Time & Calendar* to use adjectives in agreement with quantities and dates, and to *Past Tenses: Passato Prossimo & Imperfetto* where past-participle adjectives also need agreement.

# Numbers, Time & Calendar

Numbers, time and dates are the most-used "facts" in any language: prices, ages, addresses, train schedules, birthdays. Italian numbers are mostly regular but gain accents on multiples of ten ending in tre, and time is told on a 24-hour clock in writing while spoken use is often 12-hour with *del mattino* / *di sera*.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| zero | 0 | DZEH-roh |
| uno, due, tre | 1, 2, 3 | OO-noh, DOO-eh, TREH |
| quattro, cinque, sei | 4, 5, 6 | KWAT-troh, CHEEN-kweh, SEH-ee |
| sette, otto, nove | 7, 8, 9 | SET-teh, OT-toh, NOH-veh |
| dieci, undici, dodici | 10, 11, 12 | DYEH-chee, OON-dee-chee |
| venti, ventuno, ventitré | 20, 21, 23 | drops final vowel before *uno*/*otto*; *tré* always accented |
| trenta, quaranta, cinquanta | 30, 40, 50 | regular -anta pattern |
| cento, mille, un milione | 100, 1000, 1,000,000 | plural: *due mila*, *due milioni* |
| primo, secondo, terzo | first, second, third | ordinals agree in gender/number |
| che ora è? / che ore sono? | what time is it? | singular for 1 o'clock, plural otherwise |
| sono le tre | it is three o'clock | feminine plural *le ore* implied |
| è l'una | it is one o'clock | singular |
| mezzogiorno / mezzanotte | noon / midnight | meh-dzoh-JOR-noh |
| e un quarto / e mezza | quarter past / half past | *le tre e un quarto* = 3:15 |
| meno un quarto | quarter to | *le tre meno un quarto* = 2:45 |
| lunedì, martedì, mercoledì | Mon, Tue, Wed | days lowercase, accented final *-ì* |
| giovedì, venerdì | Thu, Fri | jhoh-veh-DEE, veh-ner-DEE |
| sabato, domenica | Sat, Sun | only these two end in vowel |
| gennaio, febbraio, marzo | Jan, Feb, Mar | months lowercase |
| aprile, maggio, giugno | Apr, May, Jun | |
| luglio, agosto, settembre | Jul, Aug, Sep | |
| ottobre, novembre, dicembre | Oct, Nov, Dec | |
| primavera, estate, autunno, inverno | spring, summer, autumn, winter | |
| oggi, ieri, domani | today, yesterday, tomorrow | |
| dopodomani / l'altroieri | day after tomorrow / day before yesterday | |

## Example Sentences

- **Sono le otto e mezza.** — It is half past eight.
- **Il treno parte alle quattordici e dieci.** — The train leaves at 14:10.
- **Quanto costa? — Trentasette euro e cinquanta.** — How much? Thirty-seven euros fifty.
- **Il mio compleanno è il diciotto giugno.** — My birthday is June 18th.
- **Oggi è lunedì, domani è martedì.** — Today is Monday, tomorrow is Tuesday.
- **Mio nonno ha novantadue anni.** — My grandfather is ninety-two years old.
- **Ci vediamo alle sette di sera.** — See you at seven in the evening.
- **A che ora apre il negozio? — Alle nove e un quarto.** — What time does the shop open? At 9:15.

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Counting on the tens.** When *uno* (1) or *otto* (8) follows a tens word, the tens word drops its final vowel: *venti + uno → ventuno*, *trenta + otto → trentotto*. Note also that any tens-word + *tre* takes a written accent: *ventitré*, *trentatré*, *quarantatré*.

**Hundreds and thousands.** *Cento* is invariable: *duecento*, *trecento*. But *mille* becomes *mila* in the plural: *duemila*, *tremila*. And *milione* / *miliardo* take *di* before a noun: *un milione di abitanti* (a million inhabitants).

**Telling time.** Italians use *è* for one o'clock, noon, and midnight (singular) and *sono* for everything else (plural, agreeing with implied *le ore*). The 24-hour clock dominates schedules and official contexts; informal speech often uses 12-hour with *di mattina* (morning), *di pomeriggio* (afternoon), *di sera* (evening), *di notte* (late night).

**Dates.** Italian uses cardinal numbers for all dates *except* the first of the month, which is ordinal: *il primo maggio*, but *il due maggio*, *il tre maggio*, etc. The format is day-month-year: *15/03/2024* = March 15.

**Days and months are lowercase** in Italian (unlike English): *lunedì*, *gennaio*. Days end in stressed *-ì* except *sabato* and *domenica*.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't say** *trenta-tre* without the accent — it must be *trentatré* (one word, accented).
- **Don't capitalize** days or months: write *lunedì*, not *Lunedì*.
- **Avoid** saying *uno euro* — when counting nouns, use *un euro* (the apocopated form), and similarly *un anno*, *un libro*.
- **Don't forget** the article with time: *alle otto* (at 8), not *a otto*.
- **Watch the false friend** *mille* — it means 1,000, not 1,000,000. A million is *un milione*.

## Try It Yourself

1. Count from 70 to 100 aloud: *settanta, settantuno, settantadue, settantatré...*
2. Tell the time right now in two ways: 24-hour written form and 12-hour spoken form.
3. Say your birthday in Italian: *Il mio compleanno è il [day] [month].*
4. Read these prices aloud: €4,50 — €127 — €1.350 — €2.000.000.
5. Write today's date in Italian format and read it out loud.

## Next Steps

With numbers and dates secure, move to *Food, Restaurant & Kitchen* to use them with prices and orders, and *Family, Home & Daily Routine* to build full daily-life sentences with times and weekdays.

# Food, Restaurant & Kitchen

Italy invented restaurant culture as we know it, and *cibo* (food) is at the centre of social life. The vocabulary you need splits into three layers: ingredients in the kitchen (*cucina*), the menu in the restaurant (*ristorante*), and the rituals around eating — *colazione*, *pranzo*, *cena*, the order of courses, and the tipping etiquette.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| la colazione | breakfast | usually light: coffee + cornetto |
| il pranzo | lunch | traditionally the main meal |
| la cena | dinner | often lighter, late (8–9 pm) |
| l'antipasto | starter | meats, cheeses, olives |
| il primo (piatto) | first course | pasta, rice, soup |
| il secondo (piatto) | second course | meat or fish |
| il contorno | side dish | vegetables, salad |
| il dolce | dessert | tiramisù, panna cotta, gelato |
| il caffè | coffee / espresso | always means espresso unless specified |
| il cameriere / la cameriera | waiter / waitress | |
| il conto | the bill | *Il conto, per favore* |
| il coperto | cover charge | small per-person fee |
| il menù (turistico) | (tourist) menu | fixed-price meal |
| la ricevuta / lo scontrino | receipt | |
| la pasta, gli spaghetti, le penne | pasta, spaghetti, penne | always plural |
| il riso, il risotto | rice, risotto | |
| la pizza, la focaccia | pizza, focaccia | |
| il pane, il burro, l'olio | bread, butter, oil | |
| il sale, il pepe, lo zucchero | salt, pepper, sugar | |
| la carne, il pesce, il pollo | meat, fish, chicken | |
| il manzo, il maiale, il vitello | beef, pork, veal | |
| la verdura, l'insalata | vegetables, salad | |
| la frutta, la mela, l'arancia | fruit, apple, orange | |
| l'acqua (frizzante / naturale) | water (sparkling / still) | |
| il vino (rosso / bianco) | wine (red / white) | |
| la birra | beer | |
| il bicchiere, la bottiglia | glass, bottle | |
| il piatto, la forchetta, il coltello, il cucchiaio | plate, fork, knife, spoon | |
| caldo / freddo | hot / cold | |
| dolce / salato / piccante | sweet / salty / spicy | |
| crudo / cotto | raw / cooked | |
| Vorrei... | I would like... | polite ordering verb |
| Ha... ? | Do you have...? | formal *Lei* form |
| Sono allergico/a a... | I'm allergic to... | agree with speaker's gender |

## Example Sentences

- **Vorrei un tavolo per due, per favore.** — I'd like a table for two, please.
- **Che cosa mi consiglia oggi?** — What do you recommend today? (formal)
- **Per primo prendo gli spaghetti alla carbonara.** — For the first course I'll have spaghetti carbonara.
- **Per secondo, una bistecca al sangue, per piacere.** — For the second course, a rare steak, please.
- **Sono vegetariano, c'è qualcosa senza carne?** — I'm vegetarian, is there something without meat?
- **Mi può portare un bicchiere d'acqua naturale?** — Can you bring me a glass of still water? (formal)
- **Il conto, per favore. Possiamo pagare con la carta?** — The bill, please. Can we pay by card?
- **Buon appetito!** — Enjoy your meal!

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Articles with food.** Italian uses the definite article more than English: *Mi piace il caffè* (I like coffee), *La pasta è pronta* (The pasta is ready). When asking generally for "some" of an uncountable food, use the partitive *del / della / dei*: *del pane* (some bread), *della carne* (some meat), *dei pomodori* (some tomatoes).

**Pasta is plural.** Most pasta names are masculine plural — *gli spaghetti, i rigatoni, le penne* (feminine), *le tagliatelle*. Verbs and adjectives agree: *Gli spaghetti sono buoni*, not *è buono*.

**Ordering politely.** Use *Vorrei* (I would like — conditional of *volere*) instead of *Voglio* (I want), which sounds blunt. Add *per favore* or *per piacere*. With waiters, default to formal *Lei*: *Mi può portare...?* (Can you bring me...?), *Ha...?* (Do you have...?).

**The course order.** A traditional meal goes *antipasto → primo → secondo + contorno → dolce → caffè*. You don't have to order all of them — most diners pick two or three. Pasta is a *primo*, never a side dish to meat (that would offend a chef!).

**Tipping.** *Il coperto* (cover charge, often €1–3 per person) and sometimes *servizio* are already on the bill. Tipping beyond that is optional — Italians often leave a euro or two, not 15–20%.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't say** *un pasta* — pasta dishes use plurals: *un piatto di spaghetti*, *delle penne*.
- **Avoid** *latte* when you mean a coffee drink: in Italy, *un latte* is a glass of milk. Order *un caffellatte* or *un cappuccino*.
- **Don't ask for** parmesan on seafood pasta — it's a culinary faux pas in Italy.
- **Don't translate** "I'm hot" as *Sono caldo/a* — that means "I'm hot (sexually)". Use *Ho caldo* (literally "I have heat").
- **Watch the false friend** *peperoni* (Italian) = bell peppers, not the spicy sausage. The sausage is *salame piccante*.

## Try It Yourself

1. Compose a full meal order: antipasto, primo, secondo, contorno, dolce, plus a drink.
2. Ask for the bill three ways: standard, polite, asking to split it (*possiamo dividere il conto?*).
3. Describe your food preferences in three sentences using *mi piace / non mi piace / sono allergico a*.
4. Read a real Italian menu online and identify five dishes from each course.
5. Practice the partitive: ask for "some bread, some water, some olive oil, some salt".

## Next Steps

Move to *Family, Home & Daily Routine* to extend vocabulary into the home kitchen and the rhythm of meals, and to *Everyday Conversations* to use *vorrei* and polite questions in shops, cafés, and bars.

# Family, Home & Daily Routine

The vocabulary of *casa* (home), *famiglia* (family), and the rhythms of daily life — sleep, work, meals — gives you the words for half of any conversation. Italians live close to family well into adulthood and ask "*come sta tua mamma?*" the way English speakers ask about the weather.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| la famiglia | family | mass-noun, takes singular verb usually |
| la mamma / la madre | mom / mother | *mamma* familiar, *madre* formal |
| il papà / il padre | dad / father | papà (par-PAH), padre PAH-dreh |
| il fratello / la sorella | brother / sister | |
| il figlio / la figlia | son / daughter | |
| il marito / la moglie | husband / wife | |
| il nonno / la nonna | grandfather / grandmother | |
| lo zio / la zia | uncle / aunt | |
| il cugino / la cugina | cousin (m/f) | |
| il nipote / la nipote | nephew/grandson / niece/granddaughter | one word for both! |
| il suocero / la suocera | father-in-law / mother-in-law | |
| il cognato / la cognata | brother-in-law / sister-in-law | |
| la casa | house, home | |
| l'appartamento | apartment | |
| la stanza / la camera | room / bedroom | *camera da letto* = bedroom |
| la cucina | kitchen | also "cuisine" |
| il bagno | bathroom | |
| il salotto / il soggiorno | living room | |
| la sala da pranzo | dining room | |
| il giardino | garden | |
| il balcone / il terrazzo | balcony / terrace | |
| il letto | bed | |
| il divano | sofa | |
| il tavolo / la sedia | table / chair | |
| il frigo / il forno | fridge / oven | |
| svegliarsi | to wake up | reflexive |
| alzarsi | to get up | reflexive |
| lavarsi | to wash (oneself) | reflexive |
| vestirsi | to get dressed | reflexive |
| fare colazione | to have breakfast | |
| andare a lavoro / a scuola | to go to work / school | |
| pranzare | to have lunch | |
| cenare | to have dinner | |
| addormentarsi | to fall asleep | reflexive |

## Example Sentences

- **Vivo con i miei genitori e mio fratello.** — I live with my parents and my brother.
- **Mia nonna abita al piano di sopra.** — My grandmother lives upstairs.
- **Mi sveglio alle sette e faccio colazione in cucina.** — I wake up at seven and have breakfast in the kitchen.
- **A pranzo mangio con i miei colleghi.** — At lunch I eat with my colleagues.
- **Cosa fai stasera? — Resto a casa con la famiglia.** — What are you doing tonight? — I'm staying home with the family.
- **La camera dei bambini è in fondo al corridoio.** — The kids' room is at the end of the hallway.
- **Mio fratello e mia sorella vanno d'accordo.** — My brother and sister get along.

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Possessives without the article — only with single family members in the singular.** With one family member in the singular, drop the article: *mio padre, tua madre, suo fratello, mia zia*. With plural family members or modified ones, keep the article: *i miei genitori, la mia sorella maggiore, il loro padre* (always with *loro*). *Mamma, papà, nonno, nonna* often take the article even in singular: *la mia mamma*.

**Reflexive verbs for daily routine.** Most "morning routine" verbs are reflexive: *svegliarsi* (to wake oneself up), *alzarsi*, *lavarsi*, *vestirsi*, *pettinarsi*, *truccarsi*. Conjugate the verb and put the matching reflexive pronoun before: *mi sveglio, ti svegli, si sveglia, ci svegliamo, vi svegliate, si svegliano*.

**House vs home.** *La casa* covers both. *Andare a casa* = "to go home"; *vendere la casa* = "to sell the house". For an apartment specifically, *l'appartamento*.

**Italian floor counting starts at zero.** *Pianoterra* (ground floor), *primo piano* (first floor = American second floor), *secondo piano* (second = American third), etc. Get this wrong and you'll knock on the wrong door.

**The extended family is closer.** Italians often live near or with parents into their thirties (*mammoni* — "mama's boys" — are a national meme). Sunday lunches with *nonni* are sacred; learning the family vocabulary is a cultural insider key, not just a vocabulary list.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't say** *il mio padre* — drop the article with single family members in the singular: *mio padre*.
- **Don't drop** the article with *loro*: it's *il loro padre, la loro madre, i loro fratelli*.
- **Don't forget** the reflexive pronoun: *Sveglio alle sette* is wrong — it's *Mi sveglio alle sette*.
- **Don't translate** "I live at home" as *vivo a casa* — Italians say *vivo con i miei (genitori)* (I live with my parents) or *abito ancora a casa*.
- **Watch the false friend** *parente* (Italian) = relative, NOT parent. Parents are *i genitori*.

## Try It Yourself

1. Draw your family tree and label every member in Italian.
2. Describe your morning routine using 5 reflexive verbs in order.
3. Tour your house: name every room and one piece of furniture in each.
4. Practice possessives: *mio fratello*, *mia sorella*, *il mio fratello maggiore*, *i miei zii*.
5. Tell a story about a typical Sunday with your family in 8 sentences.

## Next Steps

Move to *Everyday Conversations* to use family vocab in real dialogue, and to *Past Tenses* to talk about your childhood and family history.

# Everyday Conversations

The bridge from textbook Italian to street Italian is conversational glue: how to keep a chat going, change topics, react with feeling, and excuse yourself politely. Italians prize a good chat (*una bella chiacchierata*); learning the connectors makes you sound human, not like a phrasebook.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Use |
|----------|---------|-----|
| Allora... | So... / Well... | filler / opener |
| Cioè | I mean / that is | clarifying |
| Insomma | basically / so-so | |
| Quindi / Dunque | so / therefore | logical link |
| Però | but | softer than *ma* |
| Magari! | I wish! / maybe! | enthusiastic agreement OR uncertain |
| Davvero? / Veramente? | Really? | reaction |
| Sul serio? | Seriously? | |
| Certo! / Certamente! | Of course! | strong agreement |
| Esatto! | Exactly! | agreement |
| Ma dai! | Come on! / No way! | mild disbelief |
| Figurati! / Si figuri! | Don't mention it! | informal/formal |
| Mi dispiace | I'm sorry | apology / sympathy |
| Peccato! | What a shame! | |
| Beh... | Well... | hesitation |
| Comunque | anyway / in any case | topic-changer |
| A proposito | by the way | |
| Senti / Senta | listen | informal/formal opener |
| Guarda / Guardi | look | informal/formal opener |
| Scusa, posso...? | Sorry, may I...? | polite request |
| Mi puoi aiutare? | Can you help me? | informal |
| Mi può aiutare? | Can you help me? | formal |
| Non capisco | I don't understand | |
| Può ripetere? | Can you repeat? | formal |
| Più lentamente, per favore | Slower, please | |
| Come si dice...? | How do you say...? | |
| Cosa significa...? | What does ... mean? | |
| Hai capito? | Did you understand? | informal |

## Example Sentences

- **Allora, raccontami della tua vacanza.** — So, tell me about your vacation.
- **Mi piace il jazz, però preferisco la musica classica.** — I like jazz, but I prefer classical music.
- **Davvero? Non lo sapevo!** — Really? I didn't know that!
- **Magari potessi venire anch'io!** — I wish I could come too!
- **Senti, hai un minuto?** — Listen, do you have a minute?
- **A proposito, hai sentito di Marco?** — By the way, have you heard about Marco?
- **Mi dispiace, ma non posso.** — I'm sorry, but I can't.
- **Cosa significa "magari"? — Significa "maybe" o "I wish".** — What does "magari" mean? — It means "maybe" or "I wish".

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Filler words are essential.** *Allora* opens a thought (≈ "so"). *Insomma* sums up (≈ "in short"). *Cioè* clarifies (≈ "I mean"). *Comunque* changes topic (≈ "anyway"). Without these, your Italian sounds clipped and unnatural — Italians use them constantly.

**Magari is uniquely Italian.** Stand-alone, it means "if only / I wish": *Vinco la lotteria? — Magari!* (Will I win the lottery? — I wish!). With a verb in the conditional or subjunctive, it means "maybe / perhaps": *Magari domani vado al mare* (Maybe tomorrow I'll go to the beach). It does NOT mean "magic" or "magical".

**Senti vs Senta, Guarda vs Guardi.** Both are imperative openers like English "Listen, ..." or "Look, ..." but with the formal-vs-informal distinction. *Senti* and *guarda* (informal *tu*); *senta* and *guardi* (formal *Lei*). Default to formal with strangers: *Senta, scusi...*

**Ma dai! is a fixed exclamation.** Word-by-word it's "but give!", but it functions as "Come on!" or "No way!" — used to express friendly disbelief, encouragement, or "stop messing around". *Ma dai, sei serio?* = "No way, are you serious?"

**Apologizing softly.** *Mi dispiace* is for both apology and sympathy: *Mi dispiace per il ritardo* (I'm sorry for the delay) and *Mi dispiace per la tua nonna* (I'm sorry about your grandmother). For mild "sorry, excuse me" passing through a crowd, use *scusi* / *scusa*.

**Active listening signals.** Italians signal they're listening with *certo, esatto, sì sì sì, ah ecco, davvero?*. Silence on the listener's side feels rude. Sprinkle these in conversation; they keep the speaker going.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't translate** *magari* literally — it has no exact English equivalent. Learn its uses by ear.
- **Don't overuse** *ma* — *però* sounds smoother in extended thought.
- **Don't say** *Sono dispiaciuto* (literally "I am sorry") — Italian uses *Mi dispiace* (it displeases me).
- **Don't translate** *figurati* as "figure (it) yourself" — it means "no problem / don't mention it".
- **Don't address** strangers with *senti* — use *senta*. Quick rule: tell yourself "older = formal".

## Try It Yourself

1. Take a 5-minute conversation in English and translate it into Italian, focusing on natural fillers (allora, però, comunque).
2. React to 5 statements with appropriate exclamations: *Davvero?, Ma dai!, Esatto!, Magari!, Peccato!*.
3. Practice asking for clarification in 3 different ways: *Come si dice... in italiano?*, *Cosa significa ...?*, *Può ripetere, per favore?*.
4. Open a conversation with a stranger using *Senta, scusi*. Open one with a friend using *Senti*.
5. Eavesdrop on a real Italian conversation (YouTube, podcast) and count the fillers.

## Next Steps

Move to *Travel & Getting Around* to use these conversational tools in real situations, and to *Formal vs Informal Speech* to master the *tu*/*Lei* register switch.

# Travel & Getting Around

Italy is a country built for travelers — high-speed rail (*Frecciarossa*) connects every major city, regional trains stop in every village, and walking through historic centers is the default mode. The vocabulary covers transit, directions, accommodation, and the language of *biglietti* (tickets) and *prenotazioni* (reservations).

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| il treno (Frecciarossa, Intercity, regionale) | train (high-speed, intercity, regional) | |
| la stazione | station | *Stazione Termini* (Rome) |
| il binario | platform / track | *binario 7* |
| il biglietto (di andata / di andata e ritorno) | ticket (one-way / round-trip) | |
| la prenotazione (obbligatoria) | reservation (required) | for high-speed trains |
| la coincidenza | connection | |
| in orario / in ritardo | on time / late | |
| convalidare il biglietto | to validate the ticket | obligatory on regional trains |
| l'autobus / la metropolitana / il tram | bus / metro / tram | |
| il taxi | taxi | airport rates are fixed |
| il volo / l'aeroporto | flight / airport | |
| la macchina / l'auto | car | |
| il pieno / la benzina | full tank / petrol | |
| il pedaggio (autostrada) | toll (highway) | |
| l'hotel / l'albergo / l'ostello / il B&B | hotel / hostel / B&B | |
| la camera (singola / doppia / matrimoniale) | room (single / double / king) | |
| la chiave | key | |
| l'ascensore | elevator | |
| la valigia / lo zaino | suitcase / backpack | |
| il bagaglio | luggage | |
| la mappa / la cartina | map | |
| la guida (turistica) | (tourist) guide | |
| il museo / la chiesa / il castello | museum / church / castle | |
| l'ufficio del turismo | tourist office | |
| la dogana / il passaporto | customs / passport | |
| diritto / a destra / a sinistra | straight / right / left | directions |
| vicino / lontano | near / far | |
| qui / lì / là | here / there | |
| sopra / sotto | above / below | |
| davanti / dietro | in front / behind | |
| dov'è...? | where is...? | |
| Quanto costa? | how much does it cost? | |
| Quanto ci vuole? | how long does it take? | |

## Example Sentences

- **Un biglietto di andata e ritorno per Firenze, per favore.** — A round-trip ticket to Florence, please.
- **A che ora parte il prossimo treno per Milano? — Alle 14:35 dal binario sette.** — When does the next train to Milan leave? — At 14:35 from platform seven.
- **Devo cambiare treno? — Sì, c'è una coincidenza a Bologna.** — Do I have to change trains? — Yes, there's a connection at Bologna.
- **Scusi, dov'è il Duomo? — Vada diritto, poi giri a destra.** — Excuse me, where is the cathedral? — Go straight, then turn right.
- **Avete una camera doppia per due notti?** — Do you have a double room for two nights?
- **A che ora è il check-out? — Alle undici.** — What time is check-out? — At eleven.
- **Quanto ci vuole a piedi? — Circa venti minuti.** — How long does it take on foot? — About twenty minutes.
- **Posso pagare con la carta? — Certo, anche con il bancomat.** — Can I pay by card? — Of course, also by debit card.

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Validate (or pay a fine).** On *regionali* (regional trains), you must stamp the ticket in a yellow/green machine on the platform before boarding — *convalidare il biglietto*. Forgetting to convalidate is the #1 tourist gotcha; the fine is around €50 even with a valid ticket. *Frecciarossa* and *Italo* tickets have a date+time printed; no validation needed.

**Asking directions: imperative or *Mi dica*?** Polite imperatives use the formal: *vada* (go), *giri* (turn), *prosegua* (continue), *attraversi* (cross). For *tu*: *vai, gira, prosegui, attraversa*. A common opener: *Scusi, mi può indicare...?* (Excuse me, could you point me to...?).

**Times and prepositions.** "At" (a time) = *alle* + plural, *all'una* (at one), *a mezzogiorno*. "From... to..." = *dalle ... alle ...*. "In" (a duration) = *fra/in* — *Il treno arriva fra dieci minuti* (in ten minutes).

**Andare vs venire.** Both translate "go/come" but differ in direction: *andare* = away from speaker; *venire* = towards. *Vado a Roma* (I'm going to Rome — speaker not in Rome). *Vieni a casa mia?* (Are you coming to my place? — speaker IS at home).

**Italian street names.** Italians say *via* (way), *viale* (avenue), *corso* (boulevard), *piazza* (square). Street numbers go at the END of the address: *Via Roma 25, Firenze*.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't forget** to validate regional train tickets — even with a valid ticket, the fine for not stamping is real and tourist-targeted.
- **Don't translate** *coincidenza* as "coincidence" — it means train *connection*. The English meaning is also valid in other contexts but watch the false friend.
- **Don't say** *al binario* when you mean "on track __" — Italian uses *dal binario* (from platform): *Il treno parte dal binario 5*.
- **Don't ask for** "the bathroom" with *il bagno* in a public building — *Dov'è la toilette?* or *Dov'è il bagno?* both work; in cafés, ask for *i servizi*.
- **Don't translate** "How long?" as *Quanto lungo?* — it's *Quanto ci vuole?* (How much [time] does it require?).

## Try It Yourself

1. Buy a train ticket in 4 lines: greet, request route, ask price, pay.
2. Give directions from your hotel to the nearest landmark using 4 imperatives (formal *Lei*).
3. Check into a hotel: greet, give name, ask room type, ask about breakfast and Wi-Fi.
4. Ask three different "How long?" questions: how long to walk, how long the train, how long the wait.
5. Read a real Trenitalia timetable online and find: a Frecciarossa, an Intercity, a regionale to one destination.

## Next Steps

Move to *Formal vs Informal Speech* for the register choices that matter when asking strangers for help, and to *Italian Cuisine & Regional Culture* to read menus and engage with regional food on your travels.

# Formal vs Informal Speech

Italian splits address into *tu* (informal, second-person singular) and *Lei* (formal, third-person singular). Choosing wrong is more than a grammar error — it sends a clear social signal. Get the register right and you skip past the "tourist" tier in any interaction.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano (Tu) | Italiano (Lei) | English |
|---------------|----------------|---------|
| Ciao! | Buongiorno / Salve | Hi / Hello |
| Come stai? | Come sta? | How are you? |
| Come ti chiami? | Come si chiama? | What's your name? |
| Di dove sei? | Di dov'è? | Where are you from? |
| Vuoi un caffè? | Vuole un caffè? | Want a coffee? |
| Puoi aiutarmi? | Può aiutarmi? | Can you help me? |
| Hai una penna? | Ha una penna? | Do you have a pen? |
| Sai dov'è...? | Sa dov'è...? | Do you know where ... is? |
| Mi passi il sale? | Mi passa il sale? | Would you pass the salt? |
| Cosa pensi? | Cosa pensa? | What do you think? |
| Ti piace? | Le piace? | Do you like it? |
| (a) te / per te | a Lei / per Lei | to you / for you |
| il tuo libro | il Suo libro | your book (sg) |
| i tuoi libri | i Suoi libri | your books (pl) |
| Senti! | Senta! | Listen! |
| Dimmi | Mi dica | Tell me |
| Scusami | Mi scusi | Excuse me |
| Arrivederci | ArrivederLa | Goodbye |
| Buon lavoro! | Buon lavoro! | Same — works for both |
| Grazie a te | Grazie a Lei | Thank you (back to you) |

## Example Sentences

- **Ciao Marco, come stai? — Bene, e tu?** — (informal) Hi Marco, how are you? — Well, and you?
- **Buongiorno, signora Bianchi. Come sta?** — (formal) Good morning, Mrs. Bianchi. How are you?
- **Mi scusi, Lei sa dove si trova la stazione?** — (formal) Excuse me, do you know where the station is?
- **Senti Anna, ti va di andare al cinema?** — (informal) Listen Anna, want to go to the cinema?
- **Le posso offrire un caffè, dottore?** — (formal) May I offer you a coffee, doctor?
- **Ho un regalo per te. — Per me?! Grazie!** — (informal) I have a present for you. — For me?! Thanks!
- **Posso darLe del tu?** — May I switch to *tu*? (asking permission to drop formality)

## Grammar / Usage Notes

**Lei uses 3rd-person singular conjugations.** Even though you're addressing one person, the verb is the *lei/lui* form: *Lei parla italiano?* (literally "Does she speak Italian?"). Italian historically borrowed the polite form from Spanish *Vusted*; it's an abstract reference to "Your Lordship/Ladyship".

**Capitalize Lei (formal) in writing.** In careful writing, *Lei* is capitalized when it means "you" (formal), but lowercase when it means "she": *Lei è gentile* (You are kind) vs *lei è gentile* (She is kind). In emails and professional writing this distinction is observed; in casual texts, no one bothers.

**Possessive forms also have formal versions.** Informal *il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue*; formal *il Suo, la Sua, i Suoi, le Sue*. Pronouns: object *ti* (informal) → *Le* (formal indirect) or *La* (formal direct). *Ti chiamo* (I'll call you, informal); *La chiamo* (formal).

**When to use which.** Formal *Lei*:
- Strangers, especially if they're older or in authority (shopkeepers, doctors, professors, your friend's parents).
- Anyone you address as "signor/signora" or by professional title (*dottore, professoressa, ingegnere*).
- Email exchanges with anyone you don't know personally, until they switch.

Informal *tu*:
- Friends, family, classmates, peers, children, romantic partners.
- Younger people in casual settings.
- Once explicitly invited: *Diamoci del tu?* / *Possiamo darci del tu?* (Shall we use *tu*?).

**There's also voi (formal plural).** When addressing multiple people, default to *voi* — Italian no longer uses formal plural *Loro* in most contexts (it's archaic / very business-formal). *Voi parlate italiano?* covers any group, formal or informal.

**Switching from Lei to tu.** This is a small social ceremony. The older or higher-status person may say *Diamoci del tu* (Let's use *tu*) or *Possiamo darci del tu*. After this, both switch. If neither offers, stay with *Lei*.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't use** *tu* with a shopkeeper, waiter, or anyone you don't know — even if they look young, default to *Lei* until invited otherwise.
- **Don't conjugate** verbs in 2nd person with *Lei* — *Lei parli?* is wrong; it's *Lei parla?*.
- **Don't translate** "you" as just *tu* — figure out the social context first.
- **Don't switch** between *tu* and *Lei* mid-conversation. If the other person uses *Lei* with you, mirror it. If they say *Dammi del tu*, switch and stay.
- **Don't use** *voi* with a single person to be polite — that's old-fashioned (used in some Southern dialects but standard Italian dropped it long ago).

## Try It Yourself

1. Take five sentences in informal *tu* and convert them to formal *Lei*: *Vuoi un caffè? Puoi aiutarmi? Cosa pensi? Hai tempo? Sai l'italiano?*
2. Practice greeting three people: a shopkeeper, your professor, your friend. Pick the right opener and address.
3. Ask permission to switch: *Possiamo darci del tu?* — and respond as if accepting.
4. Read 5 real Italian emails (e.g. business correspondence on the web) and identify the *Lei* forms.
5. In your next conversation with an Italian, default to *Lei* and notice if/when they invite you to switch.

## Next Steps

Move to *Reading Italian Texts* to see how register shifts in newspapers, novels, and texts, and to *Email & Formal Correspondence* to write professional Italian where *Lei* is non-negotiable.

# Reading Italian Texts

Reading is the fastest way to grow Italian vocabulary and absorb grammar implicitly. Start with structured short texts, build to news articles and short stories, and eventually reach novels and essays. The strategy: read material slightly *below* your speaking level for fluency; read material slightly *above* for growth.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| il libro / il romanzo | book / novel | |
| il racconto | short story | |
| la poesia / la lirica | poem / poetry | |
| il giornale / la rivista | newspaper / magazine | |
| il quotidiano / il settimanale | daily / weekly | |
| il titolo / il sottotitolo | title / subtitle | |
| il capitolo / il paragrafo | chapter / paragraph | |
| la frase / la parola | sentence / word | |
| il significato | meaning | |
| il vocabolario / il dizionario | vocabulary / dictionary | |
| la grammatica | grammar | |
| la trama | plot | |
| il personaggio | character | |
| l'autore / la scrittrice | author (m) / writer (f) | |
| l'editore / la casa editrice | publisher / publishing house | |
| la traduzione / l'originale | translation / original | |
| il dialogo / la descrizione | dialogue / description | |
| il narratore | narrator | |
| capire | to understand | |
| comprendere | to comprehend | |
| interpretare | to interpret | |
| sottolineare | to underline | |
| evidenziare | to highlight | |
| consultare il dizionario | to look up in the dictionary | |
| dedurre dal contesto | to deduce from context | |

## Example Sentences

- **Sto leggendo *Il nome della rosa* di Umberto Eco.** — I'm reading *The Name of the Rose* by Umberto Eco.
- **Il romanzo è ambientato in un'abbazia del XIV secolo.** — The novel is set in a 14th-century abbey.
- **Il narratore è in prima persona.** — The narrator is in the first person.
- **Non ho capito tutte le parole, ma ho capito la trama.** — I didn't understand every word, but I got the plot.
- **Cerca di dedurre il significato dal contesto prima di consultare il dizionario.** — Try to deduce the meaning from context before checking the dictionary.
- **Questa parola ha tre significati diversi.** — This word has three different meanings.
- **L'autore usa molte metafore.** — The author uses many metaphors.

## Grammar / Reading Strategy Notes

**Beginner texts to start with.** Children's books (*libri illustrati per bambini*), graded readers (*letture graduate*), comics (*Topolino, Diabolik*), and easy news sites (*Easy Italian News*, *Newsinslowitalian*) are ideal. Look for material at A2-B1 level — most words known, a few new ones.

**Intermediate progression.** Italian newspapers online (*Corriere della Sera, La Repubblica, Il Sole 24 Ore* for business). Magazines: *Focus* (general science), *L'Espresso* (politics), *Internazionale* (curated foreign press translated). Read short stories before novels: Calvino's *Marcovaldo*, Pirandello's *Novelle per un anno*.

**Approach the long sentence.** Italian likes long sentences with subordinate clauses. The strategy: find the main verb first (it's almost always second-position-ish), then identify subordinates introduced by *che, di cui, dove, quando, mentre, perché*. Translate the skeleton, then layer in the modifiers.

**Don't look up every word.** The "extensive reading" approach: skip 3-5 unknown words per page; only look up words that block comprehension or that you've seen before. Consult the dictionary at the *end* of a paragraph, not at every unknown word — this builds tolerance for ambiguity, the most underrated reading skill.

**Use cognates.** Italian shares thousands of cognates with English: *importante, intelligente, problema, dottore, università, presidente*. Trust them for first-pass meaning, then double-check the false friends (*magari, parente, fattoria, attualmente*).

**Reading aloud builds two skills at once.** It cements pronunciation and chunking (where to pause). Even at higher levels, reading aloud 10 minutes a day improves both your fluency and your accent.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't translate** word-for-word — Italian word order, especially with object pronouns and *ne/ci*, doesn't map onto English.
- **Don't quit** at the first long sentence — break it into clauses and find the main verb.
- **Don't ignore** false friends: *parente* = relative (NOT parent), *eventualmente* = possibly (NOT "eventually" in English sense), *libreria* = bookshop (NOT library — that's *biblioteca*), *attualmente* = currently (NOT "actually").
- **Don't read** only at your level — readers who only stay safe never grow. Push 10% above your comfort zone.
- **Don't skip** rereading. The second pass through a text is where most grammar locks in.

## Try It Yourself

1. Pick a children's book or graded reader at A1/A2 and read 10 pages without a dictionary. Then go back and look up 5 words.
2. Read one Italian news article a day for a week. Note 3 new words per article and use each in a sentence.
3. Read aloud a short paragraph from any Italian text and time yourself for fluency improvement over a week.
4. Practice with cognates: list 20 English-Italian cognate pairs in 5 minutes.
5. Find a poem by Ungaretti (e.g. *Mattina* — just two lines!) and memorize it.

## Next Steps

Move to *Writing Sentences & Paragraphs* to start producing your own Italian, and to *Italian Cinema, Music & Literature* for cultural context to your reading.

# Writing Sentences & Paragraphs

Writing in Italian forces you to commit to gender, tense, and word order in a way reading and listening don't. Daily writing — even three sentences — turns passive vocabulary into active vocabulary faster than any other study habit.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Note |
|----------|---------|------|
| la frase | sentence | |
| il soggetto / il predicato | subject / predicate | |
| il complemento (oggetto, indiretto) | (direct, indirect) object | |
| il paragrafo | paragraph | |
| la composizione / il tema | composition / essay | |
| la traccia | the prompt | |
| la bozza / la stesura | draft | |
| la revisione / la correzione | revision / correction | |
| la punteggiatura | punctuation | |
| la virgola, il punto, il punto e virgola | comma, period, semicolon | |
| il punto interrogativo / esclamativo | question / exclamation mark | |
| le virgolette | quotation marks | |
| il connettivo / la congiunzione | connector / conjunction | |
| inoltre / oltre a | moreover / besides | |
| tuttavia / nonostante | however / despite | |
| infatti / per esempio | indeed / for example | |
| in conclusione / per concludere | in conclusion | |
| da una parte... dall'altra | on one hand... on the other | |
| innanzitutto / per primo | first of all / firstly | |
| mentre / invece | while / instead | |
| perciò / quindi | therefore / so | |
| anche se / sebbene | even if / although | |
| affinché / perché | so that / because | |
| descrivere / narrare / argomentare | to describe / narrate / argue | |
| introdurre / sviluppare / concludere | to introduce / develop / conclude | |

## Example Sentences

- **Innanzitutto, vorrei presentarmi.** — First of all, I'd like to introduce myself.
- **Mi piace il calcio; tuttavia, preferisco la pallavolo.** — I like soccer; however, I prefer volleyball.
- **Da una parte, viaggiare è educativo. Dall'altra, è costoso.** — On one hand, traveling is educational. On the other, it's expensive.
- **Studio italiano da tre anni, perciò posso leggere romanzi semplici.** — I've been studying Italian for three years, so I can read simple novels.
- **Sebbene piova, andiamo a fare una passeggiata.** — Even though it's raining, we're going for a walk.
- **Per esempio, la pizza napoletana ha origini antiche.** — For example, Neapolitan pizza has ancient origins.
- **In conclusione, ritengo che questo sia il modo migliore.** — In conclusion, I believe this is the best way.

## Grammar / Writing Strategy Notes

**Italian sentences can be longer than English ones.** Where English breaks into shorter sentences, Italian builds longer ones with subordinate clauses linked by *che, di cui, mentre, perché, sebbene, affinché*. Don't fight this — it's a register marker. In essays and formal writing, longer is more sophisticated.

**Punctuation rules.**
- Comma before *ma, però, però* in many cases (no comma rule debate as in English).
- No comma before final *e* in lists (no Oxford comma): *pane, formaggio e vino*.
- Italian uses « » or " " for quotes; double quotes are increasingly common in informal writing.
- Capitalize only the first word of titles, plus proper nouns (*Il nome della rosa*, NOT *Il Nome Della Rosa*).
- Decimal commas, thousand periods: *1.500,75 euro* (= 1,500.75 in English).

**Paragraph structure.** Italian academic and journalistic writing follows a clear pattern: a topic sentence (*frase tematica*), supporting evidence (*esempi, dati, citazioni*), and a closing sentence linking to the next paragraph. *Innanzitutto / Inoltre / Infine* (firstly / moreover / finally) are reliable scaffolds for argumentative essays.

**Connecting devices.** Build sentences with logical glue:
- Addition: *inoltre, anche, oltre a*
- Contrast: *ma, però, tuttavia, nonostante, sebbene*
- Cause: *perché, poiché, dato che*
- Effect: *quindi, perciò, di conseguenza*
- Example: *per esempio, infatti, ad esempio*
- Time: *mentre, prima, poi, in seguito, infine*

**Drafting and revision.** Write a *bozza* (draft), then revise for: agreement (does every adjective/article match?), tense (present vs past consistency?), and connectors (do the ideas flow?). Reading aloud catches the most errors; if a sentence sounds off, it probably is.

**Style: keep verbs in agreement, watch reflexives.** A common mistake: *Mi è piaciuto* (I liked it) — agreement of past participle with reflexive in *essere*-conjugated verbs. *La pizza che ho mangiato è stata buona* — *stata* feminine because *pizza* is feminine.

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't capitalize** every word in a title — only the first word and proper nouns.
- **Don't use** the Oxford comma — Italian drops it before final *e*.
- **Don't translate** "however" as *comunque* in formal writing — *tuttavia* is the formal choice.
- **Don't break** sentences as short as English — Italian academic style uses longer, more subordinated sentences.
- **Don't neglect** agreement when you write — past participles with *essere* must agree in gender/number with the subject.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write a 5-sentence paragraph about your daily routine, using at least 3 connectors (*innanzitutto, poi, infine*).
2. Take an English paragraph and translate it into Italian, then compare with a native version (e.g. translated press articles).
3. Write a *pro/contro* paragraph: one side, then the other, ending with your view.
4. Practice punctuation: rewrite an English paragraph applying Italian rules (decimal commas, capitalization, lack of Oxford comma).
5. Keep an Italian diary — three sentences a day for a month, focusing on past tense and connectors.

## Next Steps

Move to *Email & Formal Correspondence* for the most-needed real-world writing, and to *Conditional & Subjunctive* to add nuance and politeness to your prose.

# Email & Formal Correspondence

Italian formal writing — emails, letters, applications — has stricter conventions than informal speech: rigid greetings, polished closings, and the *Lei* form throughout. Mastering 5–10 set phrases gets you 80% of the way to professional-sounding correspondence.

## Core Vocabulary

| Italiano | English | Use |
|----------|---------|-----|

## Example Sentences

- **Egregio Direttore, Le scrivo in merito alla sua offerta di lavoro pubblicata in data 15 marzo.** — Dear Director, I'm writing regarding your job offer published on March 15.
- **Gentile Dottoressa Rossi, La ringrazio per la pronta risposta.** — Dear Dr. Rossi, thank you for the prompt reply.
- **In allegato trova il mio curriculum vitae e la lettera di presentazione.** — Attached you'll find my CV and cover letter.
- **Resto a disposizione per qualsiasi chiarimento.** — I remain available for any clarifications.
- **Le porgo i miei più cordiali saluti, / Marco Bianchi** — I send you my warmest regards, / Marco Bianchi
- **Spett.le Ufficio Risorse Umane, vorrei candidarmi per la posizione di...** — Dear HR Office, I would like to apply for the position of...
- **Mi può cortesemente confermare la ricezione di questa email?** — Could you kindly confirm receipt of this email?

## Grammar / Style Notes

**Pick the opener by relationship.**
- *Egregio/Egregia* + title + surname: very formal, almost archaic. Reserve for high-status recipients (*Egregio Avvocato*).
- *Gentile* + title or *Signor/Signora* + surname: the safe formal default in business and academia.
- *Salve* / *Buongiorno*: neutral email opener; works when you don't know the recipient's name.
- *Caro/Cara* + first name: warm but professional, used after first contact.
- *Ciao*: only with people you'd address as *tu*.

**Capitalize formal pronouns in writing.** *Lei, La, Le, Suo/Sua/Suoi/Sue* — capitalized when they refer to the addressee in formal correspondence. Keeping the capital is a literacy signal.

**Closings, in order of formality.**
1. *Distinti saluti* — most formal, almost legal-document register.
2. *Cordiali saluti* — standard business-email default.
3. *Un cordiale saluto* — slightly warmer.
4. *Cordialmente* — short, neutral.
5. *Saluti* / *A presto* — semi-informal.
6. *Un abbraccio* / *Baci* — only for friends, family.

**Subject lines (Oggetto).** Be concrete and specific: *Oggetto: Richiesta di informazioni — corso di italiano* or *Oggetto: Candidatura per la posizione di [ruolo]*. Avoid vague *Ciao* or *Domanda*.

**Body conventions.** Open with one-sentence purpose: *Le scrivo per...* (I write to...). Body in clear paragraphs. Close with a "next step" line — *Resto in attesa di una Sua risposta* (I await your reply) or *La ringrazio anticipatamente* (Thank you in advance). Sign with full name; in formal letters, also include phone and address.

**Attachments and references.** *In allegato trova...* (You'll find attached...). When referencing an earlier exchange: *In riferimento alla nostra conversazione del [data]...* or *Come da accordi presi...* (As per our agreements...).

## Common Mistakes

- **Don't open** a formal email with *Ciao* unless you've already exchanged messages with that person on a *tu* basis.
- **Don't lowercase** *Lei, La, Le, Suo* in formal writing — capitalize them.
- **Don't use** *Distinti saluti* with friends — it's frigid. *Un caro saluto* or *A presto* fits.
- **Don't forget** the subject line — Italian email norms expect *Oggetto* clearly stated.
- **Don't translate** "Best" as *Il migliore* — for sign-off, use *Cordiali saluti* or *Saluti*.
- **Don't sign off** without your name — even after a formal close.

## Try It Yourself

1. Write a job-application email: opener (*Egregio*), purpose, qualifications in 3 sentences, attachments, closing.
2. Write a reply confirming receipt of an email — keep it 3 sentences max with formal close.
3. Compose a request to a professor for a meeting: greeting, reason, two proposed times, signature.
4. Practice three closings of different formality on the same email body.
5. Take an English business email and translate it into Italian, applying all conventions (Oggetto, Lei capitalized, formal closing).

## Next Steps

Move to *Italian Art, History & Architecture* and the other cultural lessons to build the cultural literacy that makes formal writing land naturally, and to *CILS/CELI Exam Preparation* for the writing tasks tested on certification exams.

# Italian Art, History & Architecture

Italy contains roughly half of UNESCO's world heritage sites and gave the world the Roman Empire, the Renaissance, and the Risorgimento. The vocabulary and historical sense help you read museum signs, navigate guided tours, and understand a culture where the past is everywhere visible.

## Core Vocabulary

| la storia | history | |

| l'Impero Romano | the Roman Empire | |
| l'Antica Roma | Ancient Rome | |
| la dinastia | dynasty | |
| il papa / il Vaticano | the pope / the Vatican | |
| la chiesa / la basilica | church / basilica | |
| la cattedrale / il duomo | cathedral | *duomo* = dome / cathedral |
| la cupola / il campanile | dome / bell tower | |
| il museo / la galleria | museum / gallery | |
| il quadro / il dipinto | painting | |
| la scultura / la statua | sculpture / statue | |
| l'affresco | fresco | painting on wet plaster |
| il mosaico | mosaic | |
| la pittura a olio | oil painting | |
| la prospettiva | perspective | invented in Renaissance Florence |
| Michelangelo, Leonardo, Raffaello | Michelangelo, Leonardo, Raphael | the High Renaissance triad |
| Caravaggio, Bernini | masters of Baroque | |
| Botticelli, Donatello | Early Renaissance masters | |
| il Colosseo, il Pantheon, il Foro Romano | Colosseum, Pantheon, Roman Forum | |
